title: Bear Gap off the Highs
teaches: The bear gap off the highs as we teach it today: a read, not a trade. The first gap down since a top that closes down 5% or more in the lower half leaves a zone of resistance. A close above the zone's top edge fills the gap and the read is off. The fall is measured, not traded; a retest short stays under the 200-day, needs the market's help, and is never taken at the gap-day close by reflex.

walkthroughs.title: VRSN, July 2008: the full window
steps: VRSN had a top on 2008-06-04. On 2008-07-07 it opened 3.4% lower and closed down 9.5% on 6.1x volume.
A full window: the day's high stayed under the prior low. The zone ran from 35.52 up to the prior close, 36.74.
On 2008-07-11 the bounce was rejected at the zone's bottom edge. That is the read.
A study short from there did well, but our ten examples are chosen winners. We teach the read, not the entry.

walkthroughs.title: DLTR, January 2020: the cleanest chart
steps: DLTR topped on 2019-10-22, then sat 5.1% off it. On 2019-11-26 it opened 14.8% lower and closed down 15.2% on 15.1x volume.
A full window with a zone from 98.98 to 112.39. The first gap since the top, and it is still open.
A flat five-week bounce rose to the 20-day, 94.25, under the 200-day. On 2020-01-02 it was rejected.
A study short did well, but the tail of the move was the 2020 market's. We teach the read, not the entry.

walkthroughs.title: CIEN, September 2017: a good gap in a strong market
steps: CIEN opened 8.7% lower on 2017-08-31 and closed down 11.0% on 11.0x volume. A textbook gap day.
Nineteen sessions later it was rejected at the 20-day EMA. The stock sat under its own 200-day, so the stock rule passed.
QQQ closed 1.0% above its 50-day. That is a strong market, so the short had no help from it.
A study short off that rejection was stopped the next session. A good gap is not enough.

questions.q: As we teach it today, what is a bear gap off the highs?
choices: A level to read, not a trade
A short to take at the close
A long to buy under the gap
A gap that will fill soon
questions.answer: A level to read, not a trade
questions.why: A level to read, not a trade. Today the app defines no trade for the bear gap. The lesson shows the level, and the fall is measured, not traded. It is never a reflex short at the gap-day close. On a stock you own, it is a warning. Any short is recommended only for traders who have already made $1 million trading.

questions.q: By our card, what does the zone over an open bear gap act as?
choices: Resistance to a rally
Support for a later long
A magnet for a quick fill
No real level at all

Schaeffer's notes a stock can fail to get through a bear gap's zone. ChartSchool says a downside breakout point becomes resistance. Bulkowski adds that gaps are weak levels, so expect a struggle there, not a wall.

wrong.No real level at all: Bulkowski calls gaps weak levels, not empty space. Schaeffer's notes stocks that cannot get through the zone.

questions.simple: It acts as resistance, because buyers trapped in the gap sell when price rallies back into it.

deeper.counter: Resistance is a tendency, not a promise. Bulkowski calls gaps places of weak support or resistance. Read the zone as a place where a rally may stall. A close above its top edge fills the gap and ends the read.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.level_resistance), though three outside publishers agree

questions.q: A bear gap day should close in the lower half of its range.
questions.why: True. Our card asks the gap day to close down at least 5% and in the lower half of its range. Fleckenstein's rules ask for the same lower-half close.
questions.lesson_line: The gap day closes in the lower half of its range.
questions.simple: True, because our card wants a weak close, in the lower half of the day's range.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.gap_day) awaiting the owner; Fleckenstein agrees on the close

questions.q: What makes a daily down gap a full window?
choices: The high is under yesterday's low
The open is under yesterday's close
The close is under yesterday's close
The open is under yesterday's high
questions.answer: The high is under yesterday's low
questions.why: The high is under yesterday's low. ChartSchool defines a down gap this way: the gap day's high is lower than the prior day's low. Our card calls it a full window, the stricter form, and all 10 scan examples were full windows.
questions.lesson_line: A full window leaves no overlap with yesterday's range.

wrong.The open is under yesterday's close: An open under the close says nothing about the day's high. A window needs the whole day under yesterday's low.
wrong.The close is under yesterday's close: A lower close alone is an ordinary down day. It leaves no empty space on the chart.
wrong.The open is under yesterday's high: That open can still sit inside yesterday's range. A window needs the day's high under yesterday's low.

questions.simple: A full window means the whole gap day stays below yesterday's low, so the two days never overlap.

reasons: full window is a proposed card term; the definition itself is ChartSchool's

questions.q: Which gap do we read first off a top?
choices: The first gap down since the top
The third gap off the same top
Any gap down in a long decline
A gap down inside a base
questions.answer: The first gap down since the top
questions.why: The first gap down since the top. Later gaps off the same top did worse.
questions.lesson_line: Read the first crack off the top, not the third.

wrong.The third gap off the same top: Later gaps off the same top did worse.
wrong.Any gap down in a long decline: Off the highs means off a top, not a decline already well under way.
wrong.A gap down inside a base: A base has no top to gap away from. The read starts from a top.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The gap day closes down at least ___ and in the lower half of its range.
questions.why: 5%. Our card's gap day closes down at least 5% from the prior close, and in the lower half of its range. Both tests must pass. Fleckenstein also wanted the close in the lower half of the day's range. The 5% line is our card's proposed line, so it may still change.
questions.lesson_line: Down at least 5%, in the lower half.
questions.simple: The gap day must close down at least 5% and in the lower half of its range.

reasons: the 5% rests on one card line (c03)
a proposed number that may change

questions.q: A stock you own gaps down off its highs. What is that gap?
choices: A warning; the stop decides
A dip; buy more shares
A risk; widen your stop
A sell signal; exit at the open
questions.why: A warning. When a stock you own gaps down off its highs, our card treats it as a warning. You manage it by your trail and the gap rule, not by a new plan. The stop is the exit and only moves up. The gap rule is the one exception. If the gap is against your stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. We never add to the position.
questions.lesson_line: A bear gap on your stock is a warning. The stop does the rest.

wrong.A dip; buy more shares: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.
wrong.A risk; widen your stop: The stop only moves up, never wider. Only the gap rule resets it.
wrong.A sell signal; exit at the open: Our card calls it a warning, managed by the trail and the gap rule. The stop is the exit.

questions.simple: It is a warning, so let your stop decide, and never add to the position.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5, B20)

questions.q: For a long, buying right under an open bear gap is a good entry.
questions.why: False. For a long, do not buy right under an open bear gap. The zone overhead is resistance, and the first rally into it is where trapped buyers sell. Wait for the fill, a close above the zone's top edge, or for a base to form under it.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy right under an open bear gap. Wait for the fill or a base.
questions.simple: False, because the open gap above is resistance, so wait for a fill or a base first.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
proposed card criterion (bg.long_warning) awaiting the owner

questions.q: A bear gap fills within days. What does a quick fill say?
choices: The buyers are strong
The sellers are strong
The gap was a partial gap
The zone is now resistance
questions.why: The buyers are strong. Our card reads a quick fill as strength. A close above the zone's top edge fills the gap. Then the level and any short are off.
questions.lesson_line: A quick fill is strength. The level is gone.

wrong.The sellers are strong: A fill means buyers took back the whole gap. The sellers lost it.
wrong.The gap was a partial gap: Partial or full says where the gap opened, not how fast it fills.
wrong.The zone is now resistance: A close above the top edge fills the gap. The level is off, not stronger.

questions.simple: A quick fill means buyers were strong enough to take back the whole gap, so the level is gone.

reasons: the key rests on one card line (c06)
the zone's top edge waits on a held decision (D-100)

questions.q: A gap that opens under yesterday's close, but not under yesterday's low, is a full window.
questions.why: False. That is a partial gap down: the open is under yesterday's close but not under yesterday's low. Our full window is stricter. The gap day's high, not just its open, must stay under yesterday's low. Then no trading at all fills the space between the two days.
questions.lesson_line: Under yesterday's close is partial. Under yesterday's low, all day, is a window.
questions.simple: False, because that is a partial gap, and a full window keeps the whole day under yesterday's low.

deeper.trap: ChartSchool's gap-trading page calls an open under yesterday's low a full gap down. Our full window asks more: the gap day's high must stay under yesterday's low too. Say a stock opens under yesterday's low, then rallies back above it. That is a full gap down by that page. By our card it leaves no window and no zone.

reasons: fixed before (a publisher counted twice)

questions.q: ChartSchool: when does a bearish breakaway gap form?
choices: After a rise, a top or a range
Near the end of a decline
After one quiet day
Midway in a fast decline
questions.answer: After a rise, a top or a range
questions.why: After a rise, a top or a range. ChartSchool says a bearish breakaway gap forms after an extended advance, an extended top or a consolidation period. A sideways range is a consolidation. Kell's DECK example fits: a gap down from highs, then a Wedge Drop, marked its 2021 top. ChartSchool calls a gap near the end of a long trend an exhaustion gap.
questions.lesson_line: Breakaway gaps down come off tops and consolidations.

wrong.Near the end of a decline: ChartSchool calls a gap near the end of a downtrend an exhaustion gap.
wrong.After one quiet day: One quiet day is not an extended advance, an extended top or a consolidation.
wrong.Midway in a fast decline: ChartSchool's list is an advance, a top or a consolidation. Mid-decline is none of them.

questions.simple: ChartSchool says a bearish breakaway gap comes after a long rise, a top or a sideways range.

reasons: the key rests mainly on one ChartSchool sentence (g02); Kell's page could not be re-read on 2026-11-12

questions.q: QuantRocket studied down gaps. Did it find small and large gaps behave alike?
choices: No; small ones tend to recover
No; big ones tend to recover
Yes; both tend to drop
Yes; both tend to recover
questions.answer: No; small ones tend to recover
questions.why: No. QuantRocket concludes that stocks tend to recover after small down gaps and keep dropping after large ones. Its first test bought just after the open and held to the close. It is one vendor's backtest, not a promise for one stock. Fleckenstein, for his short, also wanted a severe decline for that stock.
questions.lesson_line: QuantRocket: small down gaps tend to recover, large ones keep dropping.

wrong.No; big ones tend to recover: It is the reverse. QuantRocket says large down gaps tend to keep dropping.
wrong.Yes; both tend to drop: QuantRocket says small down gaps tend to recover.
wrong.Yes; both tend to recover: QuantRocket says large down gaps tend to keep dropping.

questions.simple: No, because QuantRocket says small down gaps tend to recover while large ones keep falling.

reasons: the key rests on one vendor backtest (m02), named in the stem
f03 does not speak to recovery, so it is not a second agreeing publisher

questions.q: Prior close 50.00. The gap day closes at 47.00. The close is down what percent?
questions.why: 6.0%. Divide the drop by the prior close: (50.00 - 47.00) / 50.00 is 6.0%. That clears our card's 5% line. Measure from the prior close, not from the gap day's open. The close must also sit in the lower half of the day's range, a separate test.
questions.lesson_line: Do the division. Down 6.0% clears the 5% bar.
questions.simple: The close is down 6.0%, because you divide the drop by the prior close of 50.00.

reasons: computed key

questions.q: A full window: the gap day's high is 44.00 and yesterday's low is 46.00. How wide is the window?
questions.why: 2.00. In a full window the gap day's high stays under yesterday's low, so the width is 46.00 minus 44.00. No trades took place in that space on either day. Measure from the gap day's high, not from its close or its low.
questions.lesson_line: The window runs from the gap day's high up to yesterday's low.
questions.simple: The window is 2.00 wide, the empty space between the gap day's high of 44.00 and yesterday's low of 46.00.

reasons: computed key
fixed before (LDOS's prior close was read as its low)

questions.q: What is a rejection candle?
choices: Hits the level, closes low under it
Gaps through the level and holds
Closes above the level on volume
Any red candle that nears the level
questions.answer: Hits the level, closes low under it
questions.why: It touches the level and closes back under it, in the lower half of its range. Both parts count. A touch that closes near its high shows buyers in control, not a rejection. A close above the level is a break, and above the zone's top edge it fills the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Touch the level, close back under it, low in the range.

wrong.Any red candle that nears the level: It must touch the level and close back under it, in the lower half.
wrong.Gaps through the level and holds: Holding through the level is the opposite of a rejection.
wrong.Closes above the level on volume: A close above is a break, and above the zone it fills the gap.

questions.simple: A rejection candle touches the level and then closes back under it, low in its range.

reasons: rests on one card line (c17)

questions.q: A bear gap leaves a full window. How does our lesson draw the zone?
choices: A band: gap high to prior day's low
A line at the gap day's high
A line at the prior day's low
A band: the gap day's own range
questions.answer: A band: gap high to prior day's low
questions.why: One band. By our current default, the zone runs from the gap day's high up to the prior day's low. The chart draws both edges as one zone. For an overnight gap it runs up to the prior close. A close above its top edge fills the gap. This is our current default and it may change.
questions.lesson_line: The gap zone is a band, not a line. A close over its top edge fills the gap.

wrong.A line at the gap day's high: That is the zone's bottom edge only. The zone is the whole band.
wrong.A line at the prior day's low: That is the zone's top edge only. The zone is the whole band.
wrong.A band: the gap day's own range: That is the gap day's own bar. The zone is the empty space above it, up to the prior day's low.

questions.simple: Our lesson draws the gap zone as one band, from the gap day's high up to the prior day's low.

deeper.trap: Each single line is a real edge, so it feels right. But a close above the bottom edge is not a fill. Only a close above the top edge fills the gap. Drawing one line hides that difference, so draw the whole band.

reasons: rests on one source, the card (c32, c06)
held decision D-100 (which line is the zone)
fixed before (re-keyed onto the D-100 default)

questions.q: Short the close, or wait?
choices: Wait; do not short on reflex
Short; sellers won on volume
Short, at half the usual size
Wait; short a break of today's low
questions.story: A stock gaps down 15% off its highs on 10x volume and closes near its low. The chart looks broken.
questions.answer: Wait; do not short on reflex
questions.why: Wait. Our card says never short the gap day's close by reflex. The stop over the gap day's high is wide, a median 4.2% in our test. The stock sits far under its 10-day. Big one-day drops bounced 28% on average in Bulkowski's sample. Waiting is not a promise of a later short: that needs the retest, under the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Do not short the gap-day close by reflex. Big drops bounce.

wrong.Short; sellers won on volume: Volume does not change the rule. Big one-day drops bounced 28% on average in Bulkowski's sample.
wrong.Short, at half the usual size: Size does not change the rule. Our card never shorts the gap day's close by reflex, at any size.
wrong.Wait; short a break of today's low: A plain bear gap is shorted only on the later retest, under the 200-day. A break of today's low is not that retest.

questions.simple: Wait, because a short at the close has a wide stop and big drops often bounce first.

deeper.trap: The weak close and the heavy volume feel like proof, and that is the trap. The stock sits far under its 10-day, right where big drops tend to bounce.

reasons: proposed card gate (bg.no_reflex_short) awaiting the owner; Bulkowski and Fleckenstein agree

questions.q: What do we call this?
choices: A News Failure, not a bear gap
A bear gap, since it opened 6% lower
A Parabolic Short on the bad news
A full window, a stricter bear gap
questions.story: A stock opens down 6% on bad news. By the close it is back above the prior close.
questions.answer: A News Failure, not a bear gap
questions.why: A News Failure. It opened down on bad news, then closed above the prior close: the news failed. A bear gap needs the opposite close, down 5% or more and in the lower half of the range. The open alone never decides it.
questions.lesson_line: Check the close. Back above the prior close means the news failed.

wrong.A bear gap, since it opened 6% lower: The open is not the test. A bear gap day closes down 5% or more, and this one closed higher.
wrong.A Parabolic Short on the bad news: A Parabolic Short's climax day gaps up and closes red after a burst. This one gapped down.
wrong.A full window, a stricter bear gap: A window needs the day's high under yesterday's low. This day closed above the prior close, so it overlaps.

questions.simple: It is a News Failure, because the stock opened lower on bad news but closed above yesterday's close.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
proposed lookalike line awaiting the owner
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Does the gap day qualify as a bear gap?
choices: No; the gap was bought back
Yes; it opened down more than 5%
Yes; any gap down qualifies
No; it must close down 10%
questions.story: A stock opens 6.0% lower, then buyers step in. It closes down 4.2%, at 70% of the day's range.
questions.answer: No; the gap was bought back
questions.why: No. The day opened 6.0% lower but closed down only 4.2%, at 70% of its range. Our card asks for a close down at least 5% and in the lower half. Buyers bought the gap back the same day. In our scan this near-miss read closer to a News Failure than a bear gap.
questions.lesson_line: The close is the test, not the open.

wrong.Yes; it opened down more than 5%: The open is not the test. The close is.
wrong.Yes; any gap down qualifies: The day must close weak, down 5% or more and in the lower half.

questions.simple: No, because it closed down only 4.2% and high in its range, so buyers took the gap back.

reasons: one source: our own scan and card (repo only)
proposed card criterion (bg.gap_day) awaiting the owner

questions.q: For a bear gap short, where must the stock sit against its 200-day?
choices: Under it
Above it
Right on it
Either side
questions.why: Under it. Our 200-day rule allows shorts only below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic short. A bear gap short is not a parabolic short, so it lives only under the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: No shorts above the 200-day. Under it only.

wrong.Above it: Shorts above the 200-day are barred unless it is a parabolic short. A bear gap is not one.
wrong.Right on it: The rule is under the line, not on it.
wrong.Either side: Shorts only below the 200-day. A bear gap short is not a parabolic short.

questions.simple: Under it, because our rule bars shorts above the 200-day and a bear gap short is not a parabolic short.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: A bear gap read applies to a $6 stock that trades $5 million a day.
questions.why: False. We read only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. A $6 stock trading $5 million a day fails both tests. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Price $10 or more and $20 million a day. Anything thinner is skipped.
questions.simple: False, because we only read stocks at $10 or more that trade $20 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: Fleckenstein says to short the gap-down close at once.
questions.why: False. Fleckenstein says the short seller should wait for the bounce to occur and exhaust itself. Then he shorts as the decline resumes. Bulkowski also places the short at the top of the bounce, not at the gap. Our card agrees: never short the gap day's close by reflex.
questions.lesson_line: The short comes after the bounce, not at the gap-day close.
questions.simple: False, because Fleckenstein waits for the bounce to run out and then shorts as the drop starts again.

reasons: two outside publishers agree, and the card matches

questions.q: A breakaway gap down on good volume will be filled soon.
questions.why: False. ChartSchool calls that a trap: do not assume a breakaway gap on good volume will be filled soon. Schaeffer's also notes a stock can fail to get through a bear gap's zone. So do not plan around a quick fill. The zone can stay overhead.
questions.lesson_line: Do not expect a breakaway gap on good volume to fill soon.
questions.simple: False, because ChartSchool warns not to assume a breakaway gap on good volume will be filled soon.

deeper.counter: Do not flip it into the opposite rule either. ChartSchool warns only against assuming a quick fill. A gap can still fill later.

reasons: the key rests on one ChartSchool sentence (g03)
fixed before (leaned on a different population)

questions.q: Which market reading helps a bear gap short?
choices: Red or Orange
Green or Yellow
Yellow only
Any reading works
questions.why: Red or Orange. Our card's retest short needs the market's help: a Red or Orange reading, with the stock's group weak. Our rulebook agrees: in a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. In our scan, two clean retests were stopped at once in a strong uptrend. The reading is a guide, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: A short needs a weak market. Red or Orange.

wrong.Yellow only: Yellow calls for smaller and fewer. Our card asks for Red or Orange for a short.
wrong.Any reading works: The short needs the market's help. A strong market can stop a clean short at once.
wrong.Green or Yellow: Our card asks for Red or Orange. Two clean study shorts were stopped at once in a strong uptrend.

questions.simple: Red or Orange, because our card says the short needs the market's help.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46, F65)

questions.q: In Bulkowski's falling-window study, how often did a gap show overhead resistance?
choices: 25% of the time
5% of the time
75% of the time
Almost every time
questions.why: 25% of the time. Bulkowski measured how often a minor high formed inside a falling window before price closed the gap. It happened 25% of the time. So a gap is a weak level, not a wall. Schaeffer's still notes that some stocks cannot get through the zone.
questions.lesson_line: In Bulkowski's study, a falling window showed resistance 25% of the time. A level, not a wall.

wrong.5% of the time: Too low. His page says a gap showed overhead resistance 25% of the time.
wrong.75% of the time: That flips it. 25% showed resistance, so most gaps did not.
wrong.Almost every time: No gap is a wall. Most falling windows in his sample showed no such high.

questions.simple: About 25% of the time, so most falling windows did not hold price back, which makes a gap a weak level.

deeper.counter: A gap does not need to stop every rally to matter. Bulkowski calls gaps places of weak support or resistance. Read the zone as a place where price may stall, and let a close above its top edge end the read.

reasons: the number rests on one publisher (Bulkowski)
a study statistic that can be revised
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Three up days to a high, then a gap up on day four that closes red. Which setup?
choices: Parabolic Short
Bear gap off the highs
News Failure
Parabolic Long
questions.why: Parabolic Short. Its main form is shorted on a climax day that gaps up and closes red after a burst. A plain bear gap has no burst before it, and it gaps down, not up. The direction of the gap is the tell.
questions.lesson_line: A burst, then a climax gap up, is the Parabolic Short.

wrong.Bear gap off the highs: A bear gap gaps down, and it has no burst before it.
wrong.News Failure: A News Failure opens down on bad news and closes above the prior close.
wrong.Parabolic Long: A Parabolic Long's climax gap down comes after straight lower closes. This burst was up.

questions.simple: It is a Parabolic Short, because its top day gaps up and closes red, while a bear gap gaps down.

reasons: rests on one source, the card (c23, c22)
the parabolic burst waits on held decisions (D-009, D-013)
fixed before

questions.q: Our study short in DLTR was 93.01, the stop 94.71. How far above the entry is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.8%. (94.71 - 93.01) / 93.01. A clean rejection candle gives a stop well inside the usual 3% line.
questions.lesson_line: Stop distance in percent: the gap between stop and entry, over the entry.

questions.q: Study short at 93.01, stop 94.71. Where is 3R, where a third is covered?
questions.why: 87.91. One R is the stop 94.71 minus the entry 93.01. Three of those under the entry is 87.91, where we cover a third.
questions.lesson_line: For a short, 3R sits under the entry. Mark it before the open.

questions.q: Our study ran 359 retest shorts and 311 were stopped out. What percent were stopped?
questions.why: 86.6%. 311 divided by 359. The level is a good read, but the short off it is a hard trade.
questions.lesson_line: Most study shorts were stopped. Respect the stop, not the story.

questions.q: In our study of 359 retest shorts, about what share reached 3R?
choices: About a quarter
About half
About three in four
Almost all
questions.why: About a quarter: 25.3% reached 3R and 14.2% reached 5R before the stop. It is a hard trade even when the read is right.
questions.lesson_line: Roughly one in four study shorts reached 3R.

questions.q: Which line is the zone, and for whom?
choices: Support, for a long trade
Resistance, for a short
Resistance, for a long
No level; the gap is gone
questions.story: A stock gaps up out of a base. Weeks later it falls back into the gap zone.
questions.why: Support, for a long. A gap up leaves a zone that is tested later as support, and our card calls that Gap Support. The bear gap is the mirror: a gap down whose zone is resistance. ChartSchool says the same: an upside breakout point becomes support, a downside one resistance. Same mechanics, opposite line.
questions.lesson_line: Same mechanics, opposite line. A gap up leaves support.

wrong.Resistance, for a short: That is the bear gap, a gap down. This stock gapped up.
wrong.Resistance, for a long: A gap up's zone sits under price as support, not resistance.
wrong.No level; the gap is gone: Price back in the zone is the test. Gap Support tests that zone later as support for a long.

questions.simple: It is support for a long, because a gap up leaves a zone under price that buyers defend later.

reasons: proposed lookalike line on the card; ChartSchool agrees

questions.q: Is this a bear gap short?
choices: No; shorts live under the 200-day
Yes; 12% is a big enough gap
Yes; earnings gaps tend to keep going
No; shorts are never allowed
questions.story: A leader above its rising 200-day gaps down 12% on earnings and closes in the lower half. A friend says to short it.
questions.why: No. Our rule allows a short only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short. This leader sits above a rising 200-day, so a short is off. In our scan, a gap in a stock still above its 200-day read as a pullback in a leader.
questions.lesson_line: Above a rising 200-day, a gap down in a leader is not a short.

wrong.Yes; 12% is a big enough gap: The size of the gap does not move the 200-day line. Our rule still bars the short.
wrong.No; shorts are never allowed: Our rule allows shorts below the 200-day. This leader is above it, and that is what rules it out.
wrong.Yes; earnings gaps tend to keep going: Large down gaps can keep dropping, but our rule allows no short above the 200-day.

questions.simple: No, because we only short stocks below the 200-day line, and this leader is above it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: What happened to the read?
choices: The gap filled; the read is off
The gap held; the read is on
Stronger; volume confirms the read
Not filled until it holds a week
questions.story: A stock gapped down off its highs three weeks ago. The zone runs 44.69 to 46.86. Today it closes at 47.30 on strong volume.
questions.answer: The gap filled; the read is off
questions.why: The gap filled, and the read is off. A close above the zone's top edge fills the gap. Here the zone tops at 46.86 and the stock closed at 47.30. Once the gap fills, the level and any short are off. One daily close above the edge is the test.
questions.lesson_line: A close over the zone's top edge ends the read.

wrong.The gap held; the read is on: 47.30 closed above the zone's top edge of 46.86. That is a fill.
wrong.Stronger; volume confirms the read: A strong close above the zone is buyers in control. It ends the read.
wrong.Not filled until it holds a week: Our card needs one close above the top edge, not a week of them.

questions.simple: The read is off, because the stock closed at 47.30, above the zone's top edge of 46.86, which fills the gap.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
rests on held decision D-100 (which line is the zone's top edge)

questions.q: By our card, does the market help a short here?
choices: No; it needs a Red or Orange market
Yes; the stock is under its 200-day
Yes; Yellow still allows a short
No; a 20-day rejection does not count
questions.story: A stock under its own 200-day gapped down off its highs. The bounce was rejected at the 20-day. The market reading is Yellow.
questions.answer: No; it needs a Red or Orange market
questions.why: No. The stock meets our 200-day rule, but the market rule is separate. A bear gap retest short needs a Red or Orange reading: it needs the market's help. Yellow is neither, so the short has no help.
questions.lesson_line: A good stock chart is not enough. The market must help.

wrong.Yes; the stock is under its 200-day: That meets the stock's rule. The market rule is separate: Red or Orange.
wrong.Yes; Yellow still allows a short: Our card asks for a Red or Orange reading. Yellow is neither.
wrong.No; a 20-day rejection does not count: Our card counts a bounce to the 20-day. The no comes from the market: Yellow is not Red or Orange.

questions.simple: No, because our short needs a Red or Orange market reading, and Yellow is neither.

deeper.example: CIEN, 2017: its bounce was rejected at the 20-day while the general market was in a strong uptrend. The study short was stopped the next session. The market gave no help.

reasons: rests on the card's settled market line (c14, D46/F65)
fixed twice (the scan never read the market reading itself)

questions.q: A new short here?
choices: Skip it; wait for the bounce
Short now; momentum is down
Drop it; the move is over
Short now with a tight stop
questions.story: After a gap down the stock sits 20% under its 10-day average, with no bounce yet.
questions.answer: Skip it; wait for the bounce
questions.why: Skip, and wait for the bounce. Our rule skips a short more than 10% under its 10-day average, and this stock is 20% under. 43% of the app's gap-day closes were past that line, which is the case for waiting. Skipping now does not end the read.
questions.lesson_line: Too stretched means wait. The bounce comes first.

wrong.Short now; momentum is down: Our rule skips a short more than 10% under its 10-day. This one is 20% under.
wrong.Drop it; the move is over: The rule says wait for the bounce, not forget the stock.
wrong.Short now with a tight stop: A tighter stop does not fix a stretched entry. The rule says skip.

questions.simple: Skip it for now, because a stock 20% under its 10-day average is too stretched, so wait for the bounce.

deeper.counter: Stretch is measured from the 10-day average, not from the high. A stock far off its high can sit near its 10-day after a long bounce, and that one passes this test. The rule is about distance from the 10-day, not from the top.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29 mirrored by D47)
fixed before

questions.q: With earnings four sessions away, the earnings rule blocks a new short.
questions.why: False. We take no new short within 3 sessions of a report. Four sessions away is outside that window, so this rule does not block it. The other rules still have to pass.
questions.lesson_line: No new short within 3 sessions of a report.
questions.simple: False, because the rule only blocks a new short within 3 sessions of a report, and four is outside that.

reasons: rests on one card line (c13)
rests on the owner's rulebook (B22 mirrored)

questions.q: When a bear gap short carries a high borrow fee, we skip it.
questions.why: True. We skip a short that is hard to borrow or carries a high fee. Popular collapses are often expensive to borrow. So check the borrow before any short.
questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow or a high fee means skip.
questions.simple: True, because we skip a short that is hard to borrow or carries a high fee.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D48)

questions.q: A big market flush just ended. That is a good time to press new shorts.
questions.why: False. Our card says not right after a big unwind, and never eager. Fleckenstein, too, waited for the bounce to occur and exhaust itself before he shorted. Pressing shorts into a fresh flush is the eager short the card warns against.
questions.lesson_line: Never eager to short right after a flush.
questions.simple: False, because we are never eager to short right after a big unwind, and we wait for the bounce.

reasons: the key rests on one card line (c18)

questions.q: Which bounce into the zone gives a better short read?
choices: Light volume, under the gap day's
Heavy volume, closing near its high
Rising volume on each bounce day
Any volume; price alone decides
questions.answer: Light volume, under the gap day's
questions.why: Light volume. Our card wants the bounce days to average less volume than the gap day, ideally under the 50-day average. Fleckenstein asked for the same: small gains on declining volume against the gap-down session. A strong, high-volume bounce that closes near its high means buyers are in control, and the read is off.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet bounce is weak. A loud one is buyers in control.

wrong.Heavy volume, closing near its high: That is buyers in control, which undoes the read.
wrong.Rising volume on each bounce day: Our card wants bounce volume under the gap day's, not climbing toward it.
wrong.Any volume; price alone decides: Volume matters. Fleckenstein wanted the bounce on declining volume.

questions.simple: A quiet bounce on light volume is better, because it shows little buying as price comes back up.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.light_bounce) awaiting the owner; Fleckenstein agrees

questions.q: What does this bounce tell you?
choices: Buyers are in control; stand down
Sellers are in control; press
Nothing; volume is noise
The gap has to be a partial gap
questions.story: The bounce into the zone runs on more volume than the gap day and closes near its high.
questions.answer: Buyers are in control; stand down
questions.why: Buyers are in control. A strong, high-volume bounce that closes near its high is a pass or a lower grade.
questions.lesson_line: Strong bounce, strong close: stand down.

wrong.Sellers are in control; press: A strong close near the high is buyers in control.
wrong.Nothing; volume is noise: Volume on the bounce is one of the main tells.
wrong.The gap has to be a partial gap: Partial or full is the gap's size. It does not explain the bounce.

questions.q: How do we treat the third gap?
choices: A weaker read; later gaps did worse
Best of the three; the trend is clear
Same read; each gap stands alone
Only the first gap has a zone
questions.story: A stock gapped down off a top in March and again in April. Now it gaps a third time and closes weak.
questions.answer: A weaker read; later gaps did worse
questions.why: A weaker read. Our card reads the first gap since the top. Later gaps off the same top did worse in our test. The card also warns against shorting too late in the down cycle, after several gaps off one top. A third gap still leaves a zone, but it is a weaker read.
questions.lesson_line: The first gap is the read. Later ones are late.

wrong.Best of the three; the trend is clear: A clear downtrend is late in the cycle. Our card warns against shorting after several gaps off one top.
wrong.Only the first gap has a zone: A later gap still leaves a zone. Our card simply reads the first gap since the top.
wrong.Same read; each gap stands alone: Later gaps off the same top did worse, so a third gap is not an equal read.

questions.simple: It is a weaker read, because in our test later gaps off the same top did worse than the first.

deeper.trap: Each new gap feels like more proof the stock is broken. Our card says the reverse. The first gap since the top is the read. By the third, the move is late in the down cycle, which our card warns against.

reasons: one source: the criteria card and its own test
proposed card criteria (bg.first_gap, bg.not_late) awaiting the owner

questions.q: Short or not?
choices: Not a short; it is above the 200-day
Short; the gap is the signal
Short; the bounce day rejected
Buy; gaps always fill
questions.story: A stock gapped down off a high. The bounce day closes 5.9% above its 200-day.
questions.answer: Not a short; it is above the 200-day
questions.why: Not a short. A gap in a stock still above its 200-day is a pullback in a leader. It closed 5.9% above the line.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, a gap down is a pullback, not a short.

wrong.Short; the gap is the signal: The gap is a level, and the 200-day rule bars the short.
wrong.Short; the bounce day rejected: A rejection above the 200-day is still above the line.
wrong.Buy; gaps always fill: Gaps do not always fill. Only twenty-two percent closed the gap during the bounce in Bulkowski's sample.

questions.q: What is wrong with shorting this bounce?
choices: It is late, and big drops bounce
The volume was too heavy to short
Twenty-four sessions is too long a wait
The 20-day sits above the gap zone
questions.story: A stock fell 35% on its gap day, on 27x volume. Twenty-four sessions later it bounces to the 20-day, already 40% off its high.
questions.answer: It is late, and big drops bounce
questions.why: It is late, and big drops bounce. In our scan, this BMRN short came after a 35% gap day, with the stock already 40% off its high. After a drop that large the 20-day sits far under the gap zone. So the bounce never tests the level. Our card warns against shorting too late in the down cycle. Bulkowski's big drops bounced 28% on average.
questions.lesson_line: After a big fall the 20-day is far below the zone. Late means risk.

wrong.The volume was too heavy to short: Heavy volume is part of a textbook gap. It was not the flaw here.
wrong.The 20-day sits above the gap zone: It is the reverse. After a drop this large the 20-day sits far under the zone.
wrong.Twenty-four sessions is too long a wait: DLTR was also rejected at the 20-day 24 sessions after its gap. The wait was not the flaw; the distance from the top was.

questions.simple: It is a late short, because the stock already fell 40% and big drops tend to bounce hard.

deeper.trap: The stock looks weakest here, 40% off its high, which makes a short feel safe. That is the trap. The level that matters, the gap zone, is far overhead, so the bounce to the 20-day is not a test of it. Compare DLTR: a 15% gap, then a flat five-week bounce to the 20-day under the 200-day.

reasons: proposed card criterion (bg.not_late) awaiting the owner
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Bulkowski: once the dead-cat bounce completes, what does price do?
choices: Falls again, averaging 30% lower
Rallies to a new high within weeks
Goes flat for a year or more
Fills the gap at once, on volume
questions.why: It falls again. In Bulkowski's dead-cat sample, price resumed declining once the bounce completed. It averaged 30% from the bounce high to the post-bounce low in 49 days. That is an average over his sample, not a promise for one stock. The bounce comes first.
questions.lesson_line: In Bulkowski's sample the decline resumed after the bounce, 30% on average.

wrong.Rallies to a new high within weeks: He found the decline resumes after the bounce completes.
wrong.Goes flat for a year or more: The decline resumes, averaging 30% in 49 days.
wrong.Fills the gap at once, on volume: He found the decline resumes after the bounce, not a quick fill.

questions.simple: In Bulkowski's study price fell again after the bounce, about 30% on average.

deeper.trap: The 30% is an average over his sample, not a target for one stock. The bounce came first, averaging 28% over 23 days. A short taken before the bounce would have sat through that whole rise.

reasons: the key rests on one Bulkowski sentence (b06)
fixed before

questions.q: In Bulkowski's dead-cat sample, what share closed the gap during the bounce?
questions.why: 22%. In Bulkowski's dead-cat sample, 22% closed the gap during the bounce. The figures are cumulative: 38% had closed it by 3 months and 58% by 6 months. So most gaps stayed open through the bounce. Schaeffer's also notes a stock can fail to get through a bear gap's zone.
questions.lesson_line: Most gaps stay open through the bounce.

wrong.58%: 58% is the share that closed it within 6 months, not during the bounce.
wrong.90%: Far too high. Even after 6 months, 58% had closed it.
wrong.38%: 38% is the share that had closed it by 3 months, not during the bounce.

questions.simple: Only 22% closed the gap during the bounce, so most gaps stayed open for a while.

reasons: the key rests on one publisher (Bulkowski, b05)
fixed before (the figures are cumulative)

questions.q: Kell calls a gap down from highs, followed by a Wedge Drop, a sign of a top.
questions.why: True. He says a gap down from highs, followed by a Wedge Drop, marked the 2021 top for DECK.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down from highs is a top warning.

questions.q: Which of these is the cleaner gap-day read?
choices: First gap, down 7%, lower-third close
Third gap, down 5.2%, 40% of range
First gap, down 3%, closed high
Second gap, down 6%, upper half
questions.why: The first gap, down 7%, with a close in the lower third. Our card wants the first gap since the top and a close down at least 5%. The close must also sit in the lower half. Only this choice passes all three. The others fail on a later gap, a close too high, or a drop under 5%.
questions.lesson_line: First gap, big drop, weak close.

wrong.Third gap, down 5.2%, 40% of range: The close passes, but a third gap off the same top did worse.
wrong.First gap, down 3%, closed high: The close must be down 5% or more and in the lower half.
wrong.Second gap, down 6%, upper half: A second gap did worse, and the close must be in the lower half.

questions.simple: The first gap down 7% with a weak close is cleanest, because it is the first gap and closes low.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
proposed card criteria (bg.gap_day, bg.first_gap) awaiting the owner
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: Parabolic Long; a burst down
Bear gap; it gapped off a top
Parabolic Short; a climax gap
Gap Support; a gap on volume
questions.story: Four straight lower closes, two gap downs and rising volume. The fifth day gaps down again on the heaviest volume.
questions.why: Parabolic Long. Our card says its climax gap down comes after three straight lower closes and two gap downs. This story has four lower closes and two gaps, then a third gap on the heaviest volume: a burst down. A plain bear gap has no burst before it.
questions.lesson_line: Count the down days before the gap. A burst down is Parabolic Long.

wrong.Bear gap; it gapped off a top: A plain bear gap has no burst before it. This gap came after four lower closes and two gaps.
wrong.Parabolic Short; a climax gap: A Parabolic Short's climax day gaps up after a burst up. This one gapped down.
wrong.Gap Support; a gap on volume: Gap Support is a gap up whose zone is support. This stock gapped down.

questions.simple: It is a Parabolic Long, because the gap comes at the end of a run of lower closes and gaps down.

deeper.trap: Both shapes gap down on big volume, so the last bar alone cannot tell them apart. Count what came before. A run of lower closes and gaps down is a burst, and our card buys its climax on the intraday turn. A plain bear gap has no burst before it.

reasons: one source: the criteria card
proposed lookalike line awaiting the owner

questions.q: By our current default, a bear gap is an open at least 1 ATR under the prior close, not filled that day. Read it or pass?
choices: Pass; an ordinary down day
Read it; any gap down counts
Read it; it closed red
Pass; it must open down 5%
questions.story: A stock opens 2.1% under the prior close, 0.89 ATR, and never trades back up to that close. It closes red.
questions.why: Pass. By our current default, a bear gap needs an open at least 1 ATR under the prior close, not filled that day. This open was 2.1%, or 0.89 ATR: an ordinary down day with no gap zone to defend. A red close does not make it a gap day.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1 ATR is an ordinary down day. No real gap means no zone to defend.

wrong.Read it; it closed red: A red close alone is not a gap day. The open must be at least 1 ATR under the prior close.
wrong.Read it; any gap down counts: By our current default the open must be at least 1 ATR down. This one was 0.89 ATR.
wrong.Pass; it must open down 5%: Right call, wrong reason. 5% is the gap day's close test, not the open test.

questions.simple: Pass, because the open was only 0.89 ATR down, and our default needs at least 1 ATR for a real gap.

deeper.trap: A 2.1% open can look like a gap. Size it against the stock's own ATR, not in percent alone: 0.89 ATR is under our 1 ATR line. The card's other line, 4%, fails too, since 2.1% is under it.

reasons: held decision D-099 (the gap size floor)
a provisional number that may change
fixed before

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Log it; the stop did its job
Widen the stop and short again
Short again at double size
Quit shorting for good
questions.story: A study short was taken on a clean rejection. A strong market stopped it the next day for a loss of 1R. The gap was textbook.
questions.answer: Log it; the stop did its job
questions.why: Log it. The stop is the exit and it only moves up. A textbook gap in a strong market is a planned loss of 1R.
questions.lesson_line: A planned loss is the cost of the trade. Take it and move on.

wrong.Widen the stop and short again: The stop is the exit. It never moves wider.
wrong.Short again at double size: Never add or double up. A new try needs a new setup, as a new trade.
wrong.Quit shorting for good: One planned loss is not a reason to quit. The market was the problem.

questions.q: Four study shorts lost, though each gap was textbook. What decided them?
choices: Bounce, market, distance from top
The gap size, nothing more
The date of the next report
Bad luck with the fills
questions.why: The bounce, the market and the distance from the top. In all four losing study shorts the gap itself was textbook. The losses came from what surrounded the gap. So the gap is the level, and the bounce, the market and the distance from the top decide the trade.
questions.lesson_line: The gap is the level. The surroundings decide the trade.

wrong.The gap size, nothing more: In all four the gap was textbook. Size was not the problem.
wrong.The date of the next report: Earnings timing is a separate rule. It did not decide these four.
wrong.Bad luck with the fills: Fills were not the issue. What surrounded the gap was.

questions.simple: The surroundings decided them, because each gap was textbook and the losses came from what was around it.

deeper.example: Two of the four: CIEN was stopped the next session while QQQ closed 1.0% above its 50-day. BMRN was shorted with the stock already 40% off its high. A perfect gap could not beat what surrounded it.

reasons: one source: our own scan (repo only)
scan results not yet reviewed by the owner

questions.q: What is the read, and what is left open?
choices: A clean level; the fall is not traded
A confirmed short; enter now
A buy; the gap will fill
Pass; the volume was too heavy
questions.story: A stock gaps down 15.2% on 15.1x volume, the first gap since its top. The zone is unfilled. A quiet five-week bounce reaches the 20-day, under the 200-day.
questions.answer: A clean level; the fall is not traded
questions.why: A clean level. Today the fall is measured, not traded, so we read the zone, the bounce and the market before any short.
questions.lesson_line: Read the level first. The short is a later decision.

wrong.A confirmed short; enter now: Today the app defines no trade. This is a read, not an entry.
wrong.A buy; the gap will fill: Only twenty-two percent closed the gap during the bounce in Bulkowski's sample.
wrong.Pass; the volume was too heavy: Heavy volume on the gap day is part of the read, not a flaw.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: A warning; let the stop decide
Short it against your long
Add to the long near the low
Ignore it; it is above the 200-day
questions.story: You own a leader above its rising 200-day. It gaps down 9% off its high on earnings and closes in the lower half.
questions.answer: A warning; let the stop decide
questions.why: Treat it as a warning and let the stop decide. Our card says a bear gap off highs on your stock is a warning, managed by the trail and the gap rule. The stop is the exit and only moves up, never wider. Do not add, and do not short it: we short only below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down on your leader is a warning. The stop decides.

wrong.Add to the long near the low: Our rule is the full size at one price, with no adding.
wrong.Ignore it; it is above the 200-day: The 200-day bars a short here, but the warning stands. Keep your stop and trail.
wrong.Short it against your long: We short only below the 200-day. This leader is above it.

questions.simple: Treat it as a warning and let your stop and trail manage it, because the gap warns but does not decide.

deeper.trap: The gap rule is the one time the stop can move. Our rulebook says the stop is the exit and only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception. A gap through your stop is handled by that rule, not by hope. Never widen the stop to wait for a bounce.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5, B26)

questions.q: In our test, the gap-day-close short did better with SPY under its 200-day.
questions.why: False. It did worse. In our test, the gap-day close short did worse with SPY under its 200-day. A Red market is not by itself an edge. The short needs the bounce too: never short the gap day's close by reflex.
questions.lesson_line: A weak market helps a good read. It does not rescue a reflex short.
questions.simple: False, because that short did worse with SPY under its 200-day, so a weak market alone is no edge.

deeper.trap: It sounds logical that a weak market makes any short better. Our test found the opposite for the gap-day close. A weak market helps the later retest, after the bounce fails. It does not fix a short with a wide stop into a stretched stock.

reasons: one source: the card's own test
a measured result that a new test could change

questions.q: What is the read?
choices: A first gap and a zone to watch
A confirmed short at the next open
A buy; the window will fill soon
Pass; the stall ends the read
questions.story: A stock topped, then 23 sessions later opened 7.9% lower. It closed down 13.5% on 6.7x volume and left a full window. It was its only gap down since the top. Fifteen sessions later the bounce stalled under the declining 20-day and the zone.
questions.answer: A first gap and a zone to watch
questions.why: A first gap and a zone to watch. The stock left a full window on a close 13.5% down, its first gap since the top. The bounce then stalled under the declining 20-day and the zone. Today the app defines no trade, so the lesson is the read, not an entry.
questions.lesson_line: A full window and a bounce that stalls under it: a zone to watch, not an entry.

wrong.A confirmed short at the next open: Today the app defines no trade. The lesson is the read, not an entry.
wrong.A buy; the window will fill soon: The bounce stalled under the zone. ChartSchool warns not to assume such a gap fills soon.
wrong.Pass; the stall ends the read: A stall under the zone is the read. Only a close above the zone's top edge fills the gap.

questions.simple: It is a first gap with a zone to watch, because it left a full window and the bounce stalled under it.

deeper.trap: The stalled bounce tempts you to call it a confirmed short. Our card stops at the read. A short would still need the stock under its 200-day and a Red or Orange market, and the story gives neither. The read tells you where sellers wait, not that a trade exists.

reasons: one source: our own scan (repo only)
scan results not yet reviewed by the owner
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: The VRSN study short had a stop 3.2% away. What does our stop rule say?
choices: Skip, or size down a grade
Take full size
Move the stop to the day's high
Add a second entry
questions.answer: Skip, or size down a grade
questions.why: Skip, or size down a grade. A stop more than 3% over the entry fails the usual line, and VRSN was 3.2% away.
questions.lesson_line: A stop past 3% costs grade or size.

wrong.Take full size: A stop past 3% does not earn full size.
wrong.Move the stop to the day's high: That makes it wider still. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Add a second entry: It is one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.q: Hidden ticker. Read the last bar against the gap zone and the 20-day. Read it or pass?
choices: Read it; the bounce was rejected
Pass; the gap already filled
Pass; it is above its 200-day
Read it; it closed over its 20-day
questions.answer: Read it; the bounce was rejected
questions.why: Read it. The gap day fell 15.2% on 15.1x volume and left a full window, zone 98.98 to 112.39. Price is still under the zone, so the gap is open. The bounce ran flat for five weeks to the 20-day, under the 200-day. The last bar was rejected at the 20-day EMA, 94.25. It is a read to watch, not a trade we key.
questions.lesson_line: A big gap, an open zone and a weak bounce: a clean read.

wrong.Pass; the gap already filled: Price is still under the zone. The gap is open.
wrong.Pass; it is above its 200-day: The bounce ran under the 200-day. That passes our 200-day rule.
wrong.Read it; it closed over its 20-day: It closed back under the 20-day. A rejection closes back under the level.

questions.simple: Read it, because the gap is still open and the weak bounce was turned away at the 20-day.

deeper.example: This is DLTR. The gap day of 2019-11-26 fell 15.2% on 15.1x volume and left a zone from 98.98 to 112.39. The bounce ran flat for five weeks and was rejected at the 20-day EMA, 94.25, on 2020-01-02, under the 200-day. We show it as a read; the lesson does not key a trade.

reasons: rests on one source, our dossier (d03 to d05)
fixed before

questions.q: Hidden ticker. The last bar touched the declining 20-day. Read it or pass?
choices: Pass; buyers are in control
Read it; it touched the 20-day
Read it; the gap is open
Pass; it must reach the gap zone
questions.why: Pass. The bar touched the declining 20-day but closed at 82% of its range. A rejection candle closes in the lower half of its range. This was a strong bounce into the 20-day with buyers in control, so there is no rejection to read.
questions.lesson_line: A rejection candle closes low in its range. This one did not.

wrong.Read it; it touched the 20-day: Touching the level is half of it. A rejection candle also closes low in its range.
wrong.Read it; the gap is open: An open gap is not enough. The bounce day must be rejected.
wrong.Pass; it must reach the gap zone: Right call, wrong reason. A bounce to the declining 20-day counts as a level.

questions.simple: Pass, because the bar closed high in its range, which shows buyers in control, not a rejection.

deeper.example: This is CDNS on 2024-08-09. The bar reached the declining 20-day, the right kind of level, but closed at 82% of its range. A touch alone is half a rejection. Wait for a day that closes back under the level and low in its range.

reasons: the 82% rests on one source, our dossier (d16)
fixed before

questions.q: All ten of our scanned example gaps were full windows.
questions.why: True. All 10 scan examples were full windows, the stricter form: the gap day's high stayed under the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Our clean examples were full windows, not partial gaps.

questions.q: Fleckenstein, Bulkowski and our lesson all agree on what?
choices: Wait for the bounce before any short
Short the gap-day close
Buy the gap-day low
Hold until the gap fills
questions.answer: Wait for the bounce before any short
questions.why: Wait for the bounce. Fleckenstein waits for it to exhaust itself, Bulkowski shorts the top of it, and we never short the close by reflex.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce comes before any short.

wrong.Short the gap-day close: That is the reflex short we warn against.
wrong.Buy the gap-day low: None of the three says to buy the low of a gap day.
wrong.Hold until the gap fills: A fill ends the read. None of them waits for it.

questions.q: Shorting the gap-day close and shorting the failed bounce are the same trade.
questions.why: False. The gap-day close runs into a bounce that averaged 28% for big drops. The failed bounce is a later, different entry.
questions.lesson_line: Same gap, different trade. The close and the bounce are not the same.

questions.q: Which stock had the bear gap day?
choices: Stock A; Stock B is a News Failure
Stock B; it bounced the hardest
Both; both opened down 6%
Neither; the news was priced in
questions.story: Two stocks open down 6% on bad news. Stock A closes down 5.8%, in the lower third of its range. Stock B closes 0.5% above the prior close.
questions.answer: Stock A; Stock B is a News Failure
questions.why: Stock A. It closed down more than 5% in the lower third. Stock B closed above the prior close, so the news failed.
questions.lesson_line: Same open, different close. The close names the setup.

wrong.Stock B; it bounced the hardest: A close above the prior close means the news failed. That is a buy, not a bear gap.
wrong.Both; both opened down 6%: The open is not the test. The close is.
wrong.Neither; the news was priced in: Stock A closed down 5.8% in the lower third. The bad news worked.

questions.q: Is this a full window?
choices: No; it is a partial gap down
Yes; it closed down 9%
Yes; it opened lower
No; it is a gap up
questions.story: A stock opens under yesterday's close but above yesterday's low. It sells off and closes down 9%.
questions.answer: No; it is a partial gap down
questions.why: No. It opened under yesterday's close but not under yesterday's low. That is a partial gap down, not a full window.
questions.lesson_line: A window needs the whole day under yesterday's low.

wrong.Yes; it closed down 9%: The close size does not make a window. The day's high must stay under yesterday's low.
wrong.Yes; it opened lower: A lower open alone is a partial gap at most.
wrong.No; it is a gap up: It opened lower, so it is a gap down.

questions.q: Which rules say no?
choices: The 200-day and earnings rules
Only the 200-day rule says no
Only the earnings rule says no
Neither; the read is clean
questions.story: A stock gaps down 8% off its high and closes in the lower third. It is the first gap since the top and the bounce is rejected at the 20-day. The stock is 3% above its 200-day, and its report is in 2 sessions.
questions.why: Both the 200-day and earnings rules say no. We short only below the 200-day, and this stock is 3% above it. We take no new short within 3 sessions of a report, and this one is 2 sessions away. A clean chart does not beat either rule.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart still has to pass the rules.
